title: Second-order asymptotics for the quantum and private capacities of the erasure channel
problem: The erasure channel delivers a \(d\)-level system intact with probability \(1-p\) and otherwise tells the receiver it was lost. Its quantum and private capacities are both \((1-2p)\log_2d\) for \(p<1/2\), but a capacity describes vanishing error in the limit of long blocks. At a fixed error \(\varepsilon\) and \(n\) uses, how far below \(n\) times the capacity must a code be? The Gaussian achievability term was known, and a matching quantum upper bound was known only for infidelity below one half; private communication had no matching converse.
result: For every fixed \(d\ge2\), \(0<p<1/2\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the largest code for entanglement transmission, entanglement generation or private communication (with the optimized joint fidelity criterion) satisfies \(\log_2M^*=nC+\sqrt{nV}\,\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)+O((\ln n)^2)\), with \(C=(1-2p)\log_2d\) and \(V=4p(1-p)(\log_2d)^2\). Requiring the error bound for every message keeps the Gaussian term. Fixing the ideal environment to the actual one instead changes the quantile to \(\Phi^{-1}(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon})\).
significance: This completes the second-order theory of the simplest channel whose quantum and private capacities are known exactly, at every error level and for private as well as quantum communication. It also shows that two security criteria that give the same capacity give different finite-block rates, so the choice of privacy definition is visible at order \(\sqrt n\).
limitations: The constants are not uniform as \(p\) approaches \(1/2\) or \(\varepsilon\) approaches \(0\) or \(1\), and no third-order term is identified; the converse remainder is not meant as a numerical bound at moderate block lengths. The results concern unassisted codes and joint-fidelity error measures; separate decoding and trace-distance secrecy constraints are not covered. The author states that ChatGPT was used to help develop and examine arguments, check literature, draft the text and prepare figures and computational checks.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-28: Secs. 1–3 (background, results, the communication model, Theorems 3.1–3.2, the role of conditioning on the erasure count and the proof guide), Sec. 5 in outline and the AI statement; the appendices with the averaging-matrix construction and Haar calculations were read in outline. Editorial checks: a threshold model in which a code succeeds exactly when K ≤ (n − log_d M)/2, with K ~ Bin(n, p), gives code sizes 768, 5898 and 4000 at (n, p, ε) = (1000, 0.1, 0.05), (10^4, 0.2, 0.1) and (10^4, 0.3, 0.5), against 768.8, 5897.5 and 4000 from the second-order formula; and for d = 2, p = 1/4 the formula's constants are C = 1/2, V = 3/4, as stated after Theorem 3.1. At ε = 0.05 the two quantiles are −1.645 and −1.955.
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: Each lost system goes to the environment, and each delivered system stays out of its reach. Over \(n\) uses with \(K\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) losses, the receiver holds \(n-K\) systems and the environment \(K\), which suggests the balance \(\log_dM\approx(n-K)-K=n-2K\). Since \(K\) has mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\), the code size should be \(n(1-2p)\log_2d\) minus a Gaussian fluctuation of standard deviation \(2\sqrt{np(1-p)}\log_2d\), placed at the \(\varepsilon\) quantile.

That heuristic fails for an individual pattern. With \(n=4\), one erasure and \(M=d^3\), an encoder can put its three logical systems in positions \(2,3,4\) and recover perfectly if position \(1\) is lost, beating \(n-2k=2\). The same encoder must also survive the other three single erasures, so a converse has to control the average fidelity over all patterns of a given size, not each one.

Erasure flags let the decoder read the lost set first, and the paper shows that the optimized private fidelity, and the entanglement fidelity, are exact binomial averages of the conditional fidelities over the erasure count. The main estimate, an averaged Singleton bound for privacy tests (Theorem 5.2), states that if \(\log_dM\ge n-2k+h_n\) with \(h_n=O((\ln n)^2)\), the fidelity averaged over size-\(k\) patterns is at most \(3n^{-2}\). The binomial distribution then turns this into the Gaussian converse. Entanglement transmission yields private codes at the same error, so the private converse also bounds the quantum tasks.

The achievability side uses a Haar-random isometry encoding with a maximally entangled input, following Can and Wilde, and gives a constant-order loss. The marginal-environment criterion differs because a code that is perfect on patterns of total probability \(s\) and useless on the rest has optimized fidelity \(s\) but marginal fidelity \(s^2\); the requirement \(s\ge\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\) instead of \(s\ge1-\varepsilon\) shifts the quantile.

methods.explanation: The channel's randomness is entirely in which systems are lost, and the receiver learns that set. Conditioning on it removes \(p\) from the communication problem and leaves a family of deterministic problems that share one encoder; only binomial weights remain.
math: For an erased set \(E\), let \(f_E\) be the conditional optimized private fidelity and \(\overline f_{n,k}\) its average over the \(\binom nk\) sets of size \(k\). Lemma 4.1 proves \[f_{\mathrm{opt}}=\mathbb E_K\,\overline f_{n,K},\qquad K\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p),\] and the same identity holds for entanglement fidelity by linearity. The private identity is not linearity: it requires optimizing the ideal environment's weight on each flag pattern, which the definition of \(f_{\mathrm{opt}}\) allows.

Editorial sketch of the Gaussian step: if \(\overline f_{n,k}\le3n^{-2}\) whenever \(k>(n-\log_dM-h_n)/2\), then \(1-\varepsilon\le f_{\mathrm{opt}}\le\Pr[K\le k^*]+3n^{-2}\) with \(k^*=(n-\log_dM-h_n)/2\). By the central limit theorem, \(\Pr[K\le k^*]\ge1-\varepsilon-o(1)\) forces \(k^*\ge np+\sqrt{np(1-p)}\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)-O(1)\), which rearranges to \[\log_dM\le n(1-2p)+2\sqrt{np(1-p)}\,\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)+h_n+O(1).\] Editorial check: this threshold model reproduces the formula to within one unit of \(\log_2M\) at \(n=1000\) and \(n=10^4\).
methods.transfer: Any channel that announces a classical index of the noise realization, such as flagged depolarizing channels or channels with known loss in photonic links, admits the same reduction to a family of fixed-noise problems weighted by a known distribution.

methods.technique: An averaged Singleton bound for privacy tests
methods.explanation: The quantum Singleton bound \(\log_dM\le n-2k\) holds for codes that correct every size-\(k\) erasure exactly. At a fixed error one needs an approximate version for codes that do well on average over patterns, robust enough to force the average fidelity to vanish once the bound is exceeded by a small margin.
math: Each conditional private fidelity is bounded by the acceptance probability of a privacy test, a projector that checks correct decoding and independence from the environment. Two such tests for sets \(E\) and \(E'\) overlap by at most \(\dim(\text{shared receiver input})/M\), following Wilde's earlier lemmas. If the receiver keeps \(n-k\) systems in each case, a large \(M\) forces nearly orthogonal tests whenever the surviving sets overlap little.

To turn pairwise overlaps into an average bound, the paper builds a signed averaging matrix on size-\(k\) subsets from a biased tensor-product construction and a Meixner polynomial identity, with small support and small absolute row sums. The result, Theorem 5.2, is \[\log_dM\ge n-2k+h_n\ \Longrightarrow\ \overline f_{n,k}\le3n^{-2},\qquad h_n=O((\ln n)^2),\] for all \(k\le p_0n\) above an \(O(\ln n)\) cutoff, with \(p<p_0<1/2\). The \((\ln n)^2\) margin is the source of the converse remainder.
methods.transfer: Averaged Singleton-type bounds over random subsets apply to approximate quantum codes, secret sharing and quantum storage with random loss, wherever the requirement is good recovery for most, not all, erasure patterns.
